strengths: The paper addresses an important clinical NLP resource gap: 8,767 synthetic examples covering 15 categories, with spans, presence, temporality, and rationales. Broad coverage and public availability offer practical value beyond the relatively simple generation method.

The classification results support the usefulness of synthetic-data initialization. On MIMIC-SBDH-aligned, RoBERTa macro-F improves from 59.27 to 65.05 with standard fine-tuning and from 55.64 to 91.11 with prompt-based fine-tuning. Multiple architectures, three-run reporting, and low-resource experiments strengthen this evidence.

Expert involvement is substantial: two experienced annotators review all 1,755 synthetic test examples, correct annotations and rationales, and adjudicate disagreements. The category-specific error analysis makes the dataset's limitations more transparent.

The generation prompts, 45 seed examples, annotation guidelines, preprocessing descriptions, and training configurations support reproducibility. The stated release of data and checkpoints, together with demonstrated real-data utility, supports a Findings recommendation.
weaknesses: The broad claim of consistent improvement exceeds the results. Full-data VA NER gains are small for established baselines: RoBERTa macro-F decreases from 67.99 to 67.87, while FLAN-T5 improves from 64.93 to 66.34. The spectacular T5 gain starts from a highly unstable baseline, and Table 14 shows little benefit for Llama models. Generalization is evaluated after target-domain fine-tuning, which supports a narrower claim about transferable initialization.

The largest rare-category result needs stronger uncertainty analysis. Housing insecurity has only 18 positive test examples and accounts for approximately two-thirds of the prompt-based RoBERTa macro-F increase. Variation across three training runs does not capture uncertainty from this small test sample. Test-sample confidence intervals and class-balancing baselines would strengthen the interpretation.

Annotation quality is uneven, and the agreement comparison needs clarification. The reported 71.06% is 2,478 retained annotations divided by 3,487 annotations including human additions; its comparability with 77.80% human agreement is insufficiently explained. Moreover, Appendix E.2 accepts an existing GPT-selected category where a newly added annotation would receive a different, more specific category. A blinded audit would better establish consistency independently of the generated labels.

The rationale-distillation claim has limited support. Macro-F gains are only 0.66 and 0.58 points for T5 and FLAN-T5, respectively, with the latter nonsignificant (p=0.36). Evaluation is confined to the synthetic test set. These results provide preliminary evidence for auxiliary rationale supervision, but do not establish transferred reasoning capability or improved extraction on real clinical text.

Several reporting inconsistencies require correction. Appendix D.1 treats Table 13 as comparing training with versus without Synth-SBDH, whereas D.2 and its caption describe a comparison against MIMIC pretraining; the three conditions are not separately reported. The stated synthetic split counts total 8,727 rather than 8,767, and the ROUGE-L filtering rule ambiguously says similarity to 'all' previous examples. These issues limit reproducibility and confidence in the supplementary comparisons.
